a: by the will and power of God
p: The Armenian and Theodoret leave out the last 'of God'; Lightfoot follows them.

readings.w: Lake's text (G L and the other witnesses)
readings.en: according to the will and power of God
readings.plain: by the will and power of God

readings.w: The Armenian (A) and Theodoret, followed by Lightfoot (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: according to the will and power
readings.plain: by the divine will and power

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The meaning is the same: Lightfoot argues that Ignatius used 'will' and 'power' absolutely, of God's will and power, and that 'The addition of Θεοῦ in the common texts is a transcriber's expedient, owing to ignorance of this absolute use of θέλημα'.
b: Lake's footnote reads 'A Theodoret omit θεοῦ and are followed by Lightfoot'. It stands at the last 'of God' in the verse, after 'power' (Lake's printed page), not at 'Jesus Christ, the God' at the start of the verse.

p: One letter separates 'born' from 'come into being'; the Greek manuscript G has the second.

readings.w: Lake's text, with Theodoret; the Latin and Sahidic 'genitum' and the Armenian 'natus est' (Lightfoot's apparatus)

readings.en: truly come into being (made) from a virgin

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. Lightfoot: 'we must certainly read with Theodoret', comparing To the Ephesians 18 ('who was born and was baptized') and To the Trallians 9 ('who was truly born'). The double n comes from gennaō, 'beget, bear'; the single n from ginomai, 'come to be'.
b: Lake prints γεγεννημένον without a footnote; G's reading is from Lightfoot's apparatus, which also marks the long recension as lacking the passage ('def. g').

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the Greek.

a: joined to his flesh and his spirit
p: The Armenian reads 'his flesh and his blood'.

readings.plain: joined to his flesh and his spirit

readings.en: mingled with his flesh and blood
readings.plain: joined to his flesh and his blood

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the Greek, Latin and Sahidic. 'Flesh and spirit' is Ignatius's frequent pair (3:3; 12:2; 13:2).
b: Lightfoot gives the Armenian in Latin: 'they believed who shared in the eucharist and supped before on his body and blood', and says that 'The first clause is evidently a gloss (prob. later and certainly erroneous) of the second'.

t: 'The perfect human being' or 'who became the perfect human being'?
p: The Greek manuscript and the Latin add 'who became'.

readings.w: Lake's text (the witnesses other than G and L)
G and L (Lake's footnote: 'add. γενομένου GL')
readings.plain: the one who became the perfect human being

why: Lake's footnote names only G and L for the addition. 'Became' would make the line a statement of the incarnation (the Son became human); without it Christ is simply 'the perfect human being'.

p: Lake prints his Greek manuscript's accusative against the dative of the papyrus and the long recension.

readings.orig: εἰ γὰρ τῷ δοκεῖν ταῦτα ἐπράχθη
readings.en: for if these things were done in seeming

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake, who here keeps G against the papyrus. The sense is the same: the accusative means 'as to seeming', the dative 'in seeming'.
b: Lake's footnote: 'Here and elsewhere Bg read τῷ δοκεῖν against G which has τὸ δοκεῖν.' It stands at the first 'only in appearance' of 4:2. On 2:1 see the note there.

p: The Berlin papyrus and the Sahidic read 'says this'; the Greek manuscript, the Latin and the Armenian read 'does not say this'.

readings.w: Lake's text: the Berlin papyrus and the Sahidic (B C), Lake's footnote

why: Lake follows the papyrus. Both make sense: 'whoever says this' (that Christ was not flesh-bearing) or 'whoever does not say this' (that he was).
b: Here the papyrus, copied in the 400s (Lake), decides Lake's text.

p: The papyrus and the Armenian read 'Jesus Christ'; the Greek manuscript and the Latin 'Christ Jesus'.
why: Lake follows the papyrus. The Catechism quotes the line as 'Where there is Christ Jesus' (Catechism 830).
b: Lake's text also has the papyrus's form of 'let ... be' (ἤτω, B) for ἔστω (G g) earlier in the verse; the meaning is the same.

p: One letter separates 'you do' from 'is done'.

t: 'God is your reward' or 'God will repay you'?

why: Lake follows the papyrus, the oldest witness.
b: Lake: 'ἀμοιβή B, ἀμοιβει G, ἀμείψεται g(A), retribuat (= ἀμείβοι?) L'.

p: The papyrus reads 'Gaius Agathopus'.

readings.w: The Berlin papyrus (B) and the long recension (g), Lake's footnote

why: Lake: 'B has Γάϊον and it is possible that this, also found in g, is right, but Ῥέον is transcriptionally more probable.' A rare name like Rheus is more likely to have been changed into the common Gaius than the other way round. The same man is named in To the Philadelphians 11.

p: The Greek manuscript and the Latin read 'deacons of Christ God'.
why: Lake follows the papyrus and the Armenian. The Roberts and Donaldson English follows the other reading: 'servants of Christ our God'.
